item.title: Province launches PEI Creates to elevate Island talent with ongoing arts grant funding
item.description:
Province launches PEI Creates to elevate Island talent with ongoing arts grant funding jpranahan Wed, 08/19/2026 - 11:19

The Government of Prince Edward Island is making it easier for the world to recognize creative professionals with the launch of PEI Creates, a new brand identity to represent the Island’s creative industry, as provincial investments continue to be made towards supporting its workforce. 

Designed by One Stone Studio & Design, PEI Creates will strengthen the multidisciplinary nature of the Island’s creative industry in national and international spaces. The selected colours and design represent the Island’s natural landscapes of red soil, green fields, and blue waters, using sea glass-like silhouettes to capture the distinct geography of our province. Whether seen in the end credits of a screen production, the entrance of an art exhibit, or the back of an album, this new look will ensure projects developed in PEI or by Island creative professionals are instantly recognizable. 

“Individually, Island professionals have done a phenomenal job representing themselves in their disciplines, and our government saw a need to empower them and this sector with one cohesive brand that will help elevate the tremendous talent and creative workforce that exists here. This is an opportunity to strengthen Prince Edward Island’s competitive edge in television, film, music, and beyond."

- Minister of Economic Development, Trade and Artificial Intelligence Jenn Redmond. 

The province continues its work to support economic growth, market diversification, workforce development, and professional Island artists. This year, 64 artists are receiving a total of $211,200 this year through the PEI Arts and Indigenous Arts Grants to advance their work, contribute to the growing Island creative sector, and continue producing the high-quality work that will be represented under this new visual banner. Innovation PEI will also be recognizing the important economic, social, and cultural contributions of creative professionals at its annual PEI Arts Awards in November. The call for nominations is currently open and will close on October 5, 2026.

“Island talent can be seen through the stroke of a pen or brush, on canvases, the turn of a potter’s wheel, and on stages and screens of all sizes. This sector continues to demonstrate how creators can transform their passions into livelihoods, and as a collective, directly contribute to our economy. PEI has the talent, and this sector deserves the support and recognition of the economic force it can be,” added Redmond.

Learn more about provincial financial supports for PEI’s creative sector here.

 

Media contact:

Vicki Tse
Department of Economic Development, Innovation and Trade
vickitse@gov.pe.ca 

 

Backgrounder: 

PEI Arts Grants Recipients

First-time grant recipients are identified by an asterisk.

Charles Aondo (C. Ruth)
Music, $1,000
This project supports C. Ruth’s travel from Prince Edward Island to Toronto, Ontario, to perform at the prestigious NXNE Festival with the Mango Street Trio. Funding will help cover transportation, accommodation, and related expenses, enabling him to present his original work to national audiences. This opportunity will expand the artist’s professional profile, strengthen industry connections, and showcase PEI's vibrant music scene on a renowned international stage.

Christopher Bailey 
Writing and Publishing, $6,000
With support from this grant, Chris Bailey will create THE TRUTH IS BAD ENOUGH, a clear-eyed examination of life and fishing in eastern PEI through the firsthand experiences of the author. Based on a journal kept by Bailey in his father's final season as captain, the book expounds upon this life through entries, reflections, poetry, and visuals. Here the back of the picturesque PEI postcard is shown.

Jordan Beaulieu
Visual Arts, $2,000
With support from this Share grant, PEI artist Jordan Beaulieu will exhibit original artwork in the Atlantic Canada Zone at the 65th Toronto Outdoor Art Fair (TOAF). Taking place at Nathan Phillips Square in downtown Toronto, Ontario, from July 10 to 12, 2026, the fair will feature eight artists from the Atlantic region as part of the showcase curated by Bushra Junaid, entitled "The Land and the Sea Bind Us."

Patrick Brunet*
Visual Arts, $4,000 
Red Beds will be the artistic sum of five years of Patrick Brunet's fossil fieldwork, study and collection, brought to life through a visual art installation. A panelled ceiling-mounted mural will show the creation of the "red beds", the red sandstone cliffs, of what is now Prince Edward Island and all the snapshots of life captured within its strata 295 million years ago. Inspired by all the fossils he has discovered, Patrick Brunet will use the visual arts to share this land's prehistoric tale. To accompany the artistic installation, a program will be created. Patrick Brunet will also present an artist talk to explain the artwork and share the prehistoric and geologic story of Prince Edward Island. 

Marlene Campbell
Theatre, $7,000
With support from this Create grant, theatre artist Marlene Campbell, in partnership with Halstead Electric, will design, rehearse and present the world premiere production of the play The Conversation, touring it with professional actors to five venues across Prince Edward Island in September 2026. The Conversation tells the story of an independent and successful career woman and mother, who is not gracefully accepting the confinements of aging, and taking out her frustrations on her primary caregiver, a daughter. Both women desire more from their relationship, especially as the mother is moving towards her final chapter. But it will require each of them to become real and vulnerable. Can a mere conversation be the answer?

Nishta Gokul*
Dance, $2,000
Nishta Aadesh Gokul, an emerging Charlottetown-based Kathak dancer, will undertake an intensive training residency in July 2026 at the India School of Dance, Music & Theatre in Winnipeg. Building on nine years of guru-led study in this North Indian classical dance form, the residency will consolidate her technique for solo performance and lay the foundation for sustained Kathak presentation and teaching on Prince Edward Island.

Rebecca “Becca” Griffin
Theatre, $2,000
Catching Fish is a puppet show created by Becca Griffin and produced by Brielle Ansems with music by Jasmine Michel. This piece follows The Old Man and The Child, as they become unlikely friends with an extended cast of seabirds and fish. This 25-minute, memorable piece has no dialogue, but through movement choreographed to an original score, it is an accessible show for folks of all backgrounds and languages. With a story for all ages, Catching Fish is sure to capture your heart. The show will be presented as a scheduled production at the new children’s theatre festival, the Silly Goose Theatre Festival, taking place at Beaconsfield Carriage House from August 10 to 21, 2026. 

Adam Hill
Music, $7,000
Led by artist Adam Hill, the Charlottetown Improvisers Orchestra is a new large-ensemble project bringing together musicians from across Prince Edward Island to explore conducted improvisation, collective creation, and experimental performance. The orchestra will present three unique concerts in 2026 and 2027, including outdoor site-responsive performance, immersive spatial sound, and newly commissioned works.

Carlie Howell
Music, $8,000
With support from this Create grant, Carlie Howell will rework and expand upon their contemporary classical composition "Seeking Congruency" and arrange it for symphony orchestra. Established arranger and composer Natalie Williams-Calhoun will provide mentorship to Howell as they undertake this ambitious project.

Elder Francis Jadis
Crafts, $3,540
With support from this Create grant, Elder Francis Jadis, a respected basketmaker from Abegweit First Nation, will travel to the mainland with an apprentice to harvest Black Ash, process it and bring it back to the Island where he will pass down cultural practices and traditional basketweaving skills to younger generations in the Mi’kmaq community.

Sandy Kowalik
Interdisciplinary, $4,620
Post-war bungalows were built across Canada to house returning veterans and their families. The Alexander Drive Project chronicles the social history of one such neighbourhood built in 1948, in Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island. Interdisciplinary artist and author Sandy Kowalik blends archival research, interviews, and photographs, along with images of assemblages using found objects recovered from her garden, to create a portrait of how the street evolved, touching on themes of affordable housing. The project will culminate with the publication of a book and the presentation of a solo exhibition. 

Emmanuelle LeBlanc
Music, $5,000
With support from this Create grant, Emmanuelle LeBlanc will develop a new body of original compositions and arrangements of traditional Acadian songs through an approach that explores rhythm, voice, language and contemporary performance. Inspired by both her own compositions and the archives left by her twin sister Pastelle LeBlanc, the project will also incorporate the development of "snodhrán," an original Acadian percussive approach.

Cameron MacDuffee
Theatre, $2,500
With support from this Share grant, artist Cameron MacDuffee will present Become, an original theatrical work for one actor and four musicians exploring the theme of transformation. The piece consists of 12 original songs linked by prose exploring the theme of Becoming. The work is written by Cameron MacDuffee and publicly presented by Farmgate Theatre on August 30, 2026. 

Annie Martin
Visual Arts, $7,000
Annie Martin will create a 60-inch (5-foot) round, hand-burned and painted wall piece exploring resilience, renewal, and personal power. Funds will be used for the purchase of materials required to work at this scale and to cover documentation of the finished work through professional photography and video. This grant gives the artist dedicated time and resources to complete a technically demanding large-scale project and expand her practice into new subject matter.

Julie Pellissier-Lush
Film and Media Arts, $5,000
Through this project, Mi’kmaw artist Julie Pellissier-Lush and the Mi'kmaq Heritage Actors will give back to the community through stories, connection, and food by creating a monthly cooking class to teach community members how to preserve food and make it last longer. The classes will be filmed, and videos will be made available online afterwards. 

Robin Gislain “Gessy” Shumbusho
Film and Media Arts, $4,840
The Ones Who Stay is a portrait series and photo book documenting the real cultural fabric of Prince Edward Island. From June to October 2026, Robin Gislain Shumbusho will photograph 30 to 50 Islanders across various communities in their own spaces. The project will culminate into a professionally designed and printed photo book, distributed locally and made available to community libraries across PEI.

Reequal Smith
Dance, $6,000
Daughter in the Soil is a contemporary dance work by Bahamian artist and choreographer Reequal Smith exploring the relationship between women, land, ancestry, and resistance. Rooted in Afro-Caribbean movement traditions and emotional cartography, the work transforms the body into a living archive of memory, survival, ritual, and resilience through grounded movement, percussive rhythms, and embodied storytelling.

Lisa Steele*
Crafts, $1,000
With support from this professional development grant, artist Lisa Steele will attend an intensive five-day pottery course to expand into more advanced throwing technical pottery skills and learn about smoke and primitive firing in a downdraft barrel kiln. These new skills will benefit her work in pottery in PEI.

Zac Thompson
Writing and Publishing, $5,000
The Prison Doctor's Assistant is a neo-noir graphic novel by Zac Thompson about the weird history of so-called Canada. Set in the 1950s, it follows a med-school dropout doing hard time at Oakalla Prison Farm in British Columbia. It's here where he finds himself assisting the experimental plastic surgeries performed at the prison during this time.

Jeremy Thornhill*
Film and Media Arts, $6,500
Dearly Discarded is a poetic short film by Jeremy Thornhill that explores the relationship between consumer waste and human neglect on Prince Edward Island. The film is driven by an original spoken-word poem, an original piano score, and poetic slow-motion imagery ”from single-use garbage to dumpsters to expansive landfill sites" culminating into a quiet, human portrait of homelessness.

Maggie J. Whitten Henry*
Visual Arts, $3,500
For the month of June 2026, Maggie J. Whitten Henry will be taking up residence at The PEI Crafts Council Studios. During her residency, the artist will explore the concept of "lines" and themes of climate change (particularly "climate stripes") through textile experimentation and quilting techniques, creating an installation piece as well as guiding the creation of a community art quilt.

Natalie Williams-Calhoun
Music, $6,500
This Create grant will support the creation of string quartet arrangements to be included as part of a new “Acoustic East Coast” show that will be produced in 2027. Following on the success of the original Acoustic East Coast, this show will feature instrumental cover arrangements of favourite Canadian East Coast songs, written for the Bayfield Quartet by composer and arranger Natalie Williams-Calhoun.

item.title: Province expands support for fertility care
item.description:
Province expands support for fertility care jpranahan Tue, 08/18/2026 - 12:54

The Government of Prince Edward Island is modernizing its support for fertility treatment by giving Islanders more choice and flexibility in accessing fertility care.

Through the Fertility Treatment Funding Program, eligible applicants will now receive a lifetime maximum benefit of $20,000 per household for eligible fertility treatment expenses, regardless of household income. The new program replaces the annual funding limits and income thresholds under the previous program, allowing people to access support based on their individual treatment needs. 

"Building a family can be a long and emotional journey, and fertility treatments can come with significant costs. Making that care more affordable is one way our government can make things a little easier for people. It’s a practical approach that provides greater support for Islanders as they make personal decisions about their care.”

- Premier Rob Lantz

The program delivers on government’s commitment to modernizing fertility treatment support.  Budget 2026 included an additional $705,000 to enhance the program and help more people access fertility care funding.

"Fertility treatment doesn’t always follow a set timeline, and our program should reflect that. We heard that applicants need more flexibility when accessing support. These changes respond to that feedback and give people more choice in how and when they use the funding. This is another way we’re taking action to make healthcare more accessible for Islanders.”

- Minister of Health and Wellness Cory Deagle

Funding is available for in vitro fertilization (IVF) and intrauterine insemination (IUI) treatment expenses, including initial consultation fees and associated prescribed medications. Eligible expenses incurred on or after January 1, 2026, may also be reimbursed, if they fall within an applicant’s approved funding period from the previous Program and they have not been previously reimbursed. 

These changes followed a program review that incorporated feedback and recommendations from fertility advocates and community partners. Recommendations included removing income limits, increasing available funding, and expanding eligible expenses to cover initial consultation fees. 

More information about eligibility and how to apply, visit: Fertility Treatment Funding Program

item.title: Premier McLeod on the Enbridge Line 21 Pipeline
item.description:
YELLOWKNIFE - Premier Bob McLeod issued the following statement on the Enbridge Line 21 pipeline today:

“I was pleased to learn that operations have resumed for Enbridge’s Line 21 pipeline after almost 2 years of no activity.

"Resource development has, and will continue to be, the backbone of our economy and is central to ensuring a good source of middle class jobs and business opportunities. Our territory has mineral and petroleum resources and the development of those resources can have a transformative effect on our people and economy.

"Sustainable economic development is key to the future of Northerners. With a strong resource development base, we will be able to support diversification of our local economies into emerging and established sectors.

"On behalf of the Government of the Northwest Territories I’d like to offer my congratulations to Imperial Oil, Enbridge the town of Norman Wells and other partners for getting this pipeline back up and running. I know the efforts and economic impacts of the pipeline have already begun to take shape in the community and will be felt for years to come. ”
